label: AQ 0050
title: The recommender trained on its own clicks

questions.q: Why not just switch the target from clicks to watch time?
questions.a: It helps against clickbait, which is why YouTube's 2016 paper ranks mainly by expected watch time. But watch time is a proxy too (our reasoning: long, dull items can score well), and the model still learns only from what it chose to show. Pair a better target with exploration and a retention check.

questions.q: Exploration costs clicks today. How do you justify it?
questions.a: A small random slice is the only data where the model didn't decide what users saw, so it can score a new model fairly offline, as Li et al. did with Yahoo!'s recorded random traffic, and gives new items a chance.

teach.title: How it works: five checks and fixes

questions.q: How would you find out how strong position bias is in your feed?
questions.a: Run Joachims et al.'s swap test: for a small share of users, swap the item at slot 1 with the one at another slot. The same item's click rate in each slot shows how much the slot itself drives clicks, and gives the weights for inverse propensity scoring.

teach.title: How it works: five checks and fixes

questions.q: How can a recommender's click-through rate climb while users leave?
questions.a: A click only stands in for value: tempting items that disappoint raise it, and YouTube's 2016 paper says ranking by click rate promotes clickbait. And retraining only on reactions to its own picks can make those picks look right while the feed narrows: Chaney et al. found that in simulations, so I'd measure it in production.

questions.q: What does inverse propensity scoring do to click data?
questions.a: It weights each click by one over the probability that the user looked at that slot, so items shown low down aren't judged worse just because fewer people saw them. Joachims et al. use it to learn rankings from biased clicks.

teach.title: How it works: five checks and fixes

questions.q: What did Chaney et al.'s simulations find about retraining recommenders on their own data?
questions.a: With repeated retraining, every recommender except random made similar users consume more alike than ideal recommendations would, without a matching rise in utility, the value users get from what they consume.
